{{Short description|Poisson manifold that is also a Lie group}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Poisson–Lie group''' is a [[Poisson manifold]] that is also a [[Lie group]], with the group multiplication being compatible with the [[Poisson algebra]] structure on the manifold.

The [[infinitesimal]] counterpart of a Poisson–Lie group is a [[Lie bialgebra]], in analogy to Lie algebras as the infinitesimal counterparts of Lie groups.

Many [[quantum group]]s are quantizations of the Poisson algebra of functions on a Poisson–Lie group.

==Definition==
A '''Poisson–Lie group''' is a Lie group ''<math>G</math>'' equipped with a Poisson bracket for which the group multiplication <math>\mu:G\times G\to G</math> with <math>\mu(g_1, g_2)=g_1g_2</math> is a [[Poisson map]], where the manifold <math>G\times G</math> has been given the structure of a product Poisson manifold.

Explicitly, the following identity must hold for a Poisson–Lie group:

:<math>\{f_1,f_2\} (gg') = 
\{f_1 \circ L_g, f_2 \circ L_g\} (g') + 
\{f_1 \circ R_{g^\prime}, f_2 \circ R_{g'}\} (g)</math>

where <math>f_1</math> and <math>f_2</math> are real-valued, smooth functions on the Lie group, while ''<math>g</math>'' and ''<math>g'</math>'' are elements of the Lie group. Here, ''<math>L_g</math>'' denotes left-multiplication and ''<math>R_g</math>'' denotes right-multiplication.

If <math>\mathcal{P}</math> denotes the corresponding Poisson [[bivector]] on ''<math>G</math>'', the condition above can be equivalently stated as

:<math>\mathcal{P}(gg') = L_{g \ast}(\mathcal{P}(g')) + R_{g' \ast}(\mathcal{P}(g))</math>

In particular, taking ''<math>g = g' = e</math>'' one obtains <math>\mathcal{P}(e) = 0 </math>, or equivalently <math>\{f,g\}(e) = 0</math>. Applying [[Poisson manifold#Weinstein splitting theorem|Weinstein splitting theorem]] to ''<math>e</math>'' one sees that non-trivial Poisson-Lie structure is never symplectic, not even of constant rank.

== Poisson-Lie groups - Lie bialgebra correspondence ==
The Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> of a Poisson–Lie group has a natural structure of [[Lie coalgebra]] given by linearising the Poisson tensor <math>P: G \to TG \wedge TG</math> at the identity, i.e. <math display="inline">\delta:= d_eP: \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g} \wedge \mathfrak{g}</math> is a [[comultiplication]]. Moreover, the algebra and the coalgebra structure are compatible, i.e. <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is a [[Lie bialgebra]],

The classical [[Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence]], which gives an [[equivalence of categories]] between [[Simply connected space|simply connected]] Lie groups and finite-dimensional Lie algebras, was extended by [[Vladimir Drinfeld|Drinfeld]] to an equivalence of categories between simply connected Poisson–Lie groups and finite-dimensional Lie bialgebras.

Thanks to Drinfeld theorem, any Poisson–Lie group ''<math>G</math>'' has a '''dual Poisson–Lie group''', defined as the Poisson–Lie group integrating the dual ''<math>\mathfrak{g}^*</math>'' of its bialgebra.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Jiang-Hua |last2=Weinstein |first2=Alan |author-link2=Alan Weinstein |date=1990-01-01 |title=Poisson Lie groups, dressing transformations, and Bruhat decompositions |journal=Journal of Differential Geometry |volume=31 |issue=2 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1214444324 |s2cid=117053536 |issn=0022-040X|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kosmann-Schwarzbach |first=Y. |author-link=Yvette Kosmann-Schwarzbach |date=1996-12-01 |title=Poisson-Lie groups and beyond |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02362640 |journal=Journal of Mathematical Sciences |language=en |volume=82 |issue=6 |pages=3807–3813 |doi=10.1007/BF02362640 |s2cid=123117926 |issn=1573-8795|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite conference |conference= Proceedings of the International Center for Pure and Applied Mathematics at Pondicherry University, 8–26 January 1996|last=Kosmann-Schwarzbach |first=Y. |chapter=Lie bialgebras, poisson Lie groups and dressing transformations |author-link=Yvette Kosmann-Schwarzbach |date=1997 |title=Integrability of Nonlinear Systems |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/BFb0113695 |series=Lecture Notes in Physics |volume=495 |editor1=Y. Kosmann-Schwarzbach|editor2= B. Grammaticos|editor3= K. M. Tamizhmani |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=104–170 |doi=10.1007/BFb0113695 |isbn=978-3-540-69521-9}}</ref>

== Homomorphisms ==
A '''Poisson–Lie group homomorphism''' <math>\phi:G\to H</math> is defined to be both a Lie [[group homomorphism]] and a Poisson map. Although this is the "obvious" definition, neither left translations nor right translations are Poisson maps. Also, the inversion map <math>\iota:G\to G</math> taking <math>\iota(g)=g^{-1}</math> is not a Poisson map either, although it is an anti-Poisson map:

:<math>\{f_1 \circ \iota, f_2 \circ \iota \} = 
-\{f_1, f_2\} \circ \iota</math>

for any two smooth functions <math>f_1, f_2</math> on ''<math>G</math>''.

== Examples ==

=== Trivial examples ===

* Any [[Poisson manifold#Trivial Poisson structures|trivial Poisson structure]] on a Lie group ''<math>G</math>'' defines a Poisson–Lie group structure, whose bialgebra is simply <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> with the trivial comultiplication.
* The dual ''<math>\mathfrak{g}^*</math>'' of a Lie algebra, together with its [[Poisson manifold#Linear Poisson structures|linear Poisson structure]], is an additive Poisson–Lie group.

These two example are dual of each other via Drinfeld theorem, in the sense explained above.

=== Other examples ===
Let <math>G</math> be any [[Semisimple group|semisimple]] Lie group. Choose a maximal torus <math>T\subset G</math> and a choice of [[positive roots]]. 
Let <math>B_\pm\subset G</math> be the corresponding opposite [[Borel subgroup]]s, so that <math>T =  B_-\cap B_+</math> and there is a natural projection <math>\pi:B_\pm \to T</math>.
Then define a Lie group 
:<math>G^*:=\{ (g_-,g_+)\in B_-\times B_+\  \bigl\vert\  \pi(g_-)\pi(g_+)=1\}</math>
which is a subgroup of the product <math>B_-\times B_+</math>, and has the same dimension as <math>G</math>.

The standard Poisson–Lie group structure on ''<math>G</math>'' is determined by identifying the Lie algebra of <math>G^*</math> with the dual of 
the Lie algebra of <math>G</math>, as in the standard [[Lie bialgebra]] example.
This defines a Poisson–Lie group structure on both <math>G</math> and on the dual Poisson Lie group <math>G^*</math>. 
This is the "standard" example: the Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum group <math>U_q\mathfrak{g}</math> is a quantization of the Poisson algebra of functions on the group <math>G^*</math>.
Note that <math>G^*</math> is [[Solvable group|solvable]], whereas <math>G</math> is semisimple.
